Five Filipinos in Dubai are achieving remarkable success, including a published author and a high school graduate who became a hotelier. Izabella Faye Lebig and Ocean Thomas Tayo, both 17 years old, showcase the achievements of OFW children in Dubai. Professionals Michico Lopez Ramos, Ronin Ronald Endozo, and Michael Banua make their mark in their respective fields. This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors .
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Five Filipinos, two of them children of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), are blazing trails in this fast-paced global city.
Three of them — a businesswoman who is the lone Filipino member of a Dubai Chamber of Commerce business group, a high school graduate who earned a degree online to become a hotelier, and a social media specialist working with the Dubai government — all rose from humble beginnings.
The other two, both children of OFWs, are excelling in school. One is a published author — having written a trilogy — with immersion experience at Oxford University and a string of awards to her name; the other placed 11th overall among more than 1,000 competitors at Yale University’s World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions this month.
Seventeen-year-old Izabella Faye Lebig — deputy head of the student council at Cambridge International School Dubai who boasts a long list of achievements — is a silver awardee in the Queen’s Commonwealth Essay Competition, which drew 25,648 global entries from 54 countries.
She also received a “Very High Commendation (Top 1%)” in the law category at the UK-based John Locke Institute’s 2026 Global Essay Competition, which received more than 100,237 entries from 183 countries, according to the institute.
Moreover, Izabella Faye has won law essay-writing contests at Oxford and Cambridge Universities.
She’s the daughter of Dr. Ben Lebig Jr., a financial analyst at the Dubai office of American multinational energy firm Chevron Corp. He, himself, had come far from being a young boy who had to cross two knee-deep rivers and climb a hill just to get to school in Iloilo.
A published author, Izabella Faye wrote the Alex Hades trilogy, which she described as exploring the “theological side of fantasy… starting off as a fantasy-suspense and morphing into fantasy-action throughout the series.”
“Overall, I consider the Alex Hades trilogy… an experiment and a diary, where readers can see not only the development of the story itself, but also my development as a writer and a kid growing up,” she said.
While considering business, law, or digital marketing as potential career paths, Izabella Faye — who was once featured at the annual Emirates Literature Festival — said writing remains central to her life.
“One [thing] that I know for sure, though, is that writing will always be my thing all throughout; it’s how my mind and soul breathe, and I practically live off it,” she said.
“One thing I know for absolute certain is I’ve always wanted an opportunity to bring my stories to the big screen, and really getting involved in the production and the making of how it comes to life — it’s something I knew for sure I wanted to take part in even before I started writing,” Izabella Faye said.
“I aim for the moon, but even if I land among the stars, I’ll feel just as proud. Achievements like these, as my parents always remind me, are just one part of the journey — they are reminders of how far I’ve come, but they’re not the destination,” she said.
Another OFW child making waves is 17-year-old Ocean Thomas Tayo, who — along with teammates Jillian Denise Pilapil, and Sean Ezekiel Cosmiano — traveled to Yale University in Connecticut for the World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions.
“We were excited. We researched deeper… and met up every now and then for active recall and to try our best to soar high,” said Tayo, a 12th grader at The Philippine School Dubai, which is attended mostly by OFW children.
The team placed 11th overall in the global competition, which featured more than 1,000 participants.
The World Scholar’s Cup is an internationally recognized academic competition where individuals and teams debate, write collaboratively, and answer questions based on an annually updated curriculum. Competitors begin in regional rounds and, after passing a point threshold, qualify for global rounds before advancing to the Tournament of Champions at Yale.
Earlier, Ocean’s three-member team placed second in the Dubai Global Round, where he also finished third individually out of hundreds of scholars.
“As an Emirati [resident], I feel fulfilled. After hours and days of hard work, it really all paid off after feeling the medals and trophies, but what makes it worth it the most is bringing pride and joy to the UAE,” said Ocean, noting he had “prepared really hard — a bit too hard.”
“During the competition, I was sick the whole time. However, I still conquered and got 13 medals and seven trophies with my team,” Ocean said.
A student-leader, he founded The Pathfinder’s Project at his school, an initiative focused on personal growth, student direction, and leadership development. He was also named champion of the senior category at the Emirates Environmental Group Public Interest School Speaking Contest and won Best Debater in a simulated International Court of Justice competition.
A Filipino businesswoman, who once commuted daily from Bulacan to Far Eastern University (FEU) in Diliman during college, has been named a board member of the Printing and Publishing Business Group (PPBG) under the Dubai Chamber of Commerce (DCC).
“I am proud of having become a member of the board because I’m carrying our flag and I am the youngest as well,” said 42-year-old Michico Lopez Ramos in a mix of English and Filipino.
“Most of those sitting on the board are older because of their huge experience in the market, and all are males. Hence, I’m so flattered. I can keep up at that level with them, knowing that I’m the youngest and probably have a lot to learn.”
“I am so honored, and I know I can’t achieve this without my team supporting me,” she added.
Ramos arrived in Dubai in 2004, fresh out of college, and landed a job as a sales representative at a mobile phone and IT shop. Three years later, she ventured into opening her own digital marketing business before launching an events and advertising company in 2021.
Today, she is also co-owner of The Global Stories DXB , an online and print magazine, and the Brilliant Training Institute, which is accredited by Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA).
“My main responsibility as a board member is as sales and marketing director overseeing the group’s brand identity, social media mileage, and online presence, including press releases, website, campaigns, and other marketing collateral,” said Ramos, who holds a degree in information technology and an MBA certification in project management.
Ramos said the DCC emailed to ask if she was interested in the position.
“Of course, it involves voting, and I had to share my experience and profile. It was all God’s plan that I was chosen,” she said.
She plans to use her role to “help amplify our voices as Filipinos in the printing and publishing sector.” So far, she has spearheaded the PPBG’s logo and branding guidelines, LinkedIn and Facebook pages, and online member database, among other initiatives.
The PPBG board also includes elected and founding industry representatives such as Secretary General Hamid Maammer, Lakshmanan Ganapathy of Al Ghurair Printing & Publishing, and Roger Nicodeme of Heidelberg Gulf LLC.
Ronin Ronald Endozo of Candelaria, Quezon, went to Oman as a high school graduate at just 16 years old in 1994.
“My first three years… were some of the hardest of my life. With limited experience and skills, I struggled to find my footing and moved from one job to another just to get by,” recalled Endozo.
Now 49 years old and recently appointed general manager of a five-star luxury serviced apartment hotel, Endozo worked his share of odd jobs before pulling himself together, pursuing a college degree at 41, and reaping what he sowed.
“I worked as a garage helper, a car washer in public parking areas, a kiosk attendant, a dishwasher in a coffee shop, a catering assistant, a cargo-moving helper, a bakery helper, a meat shop attendant and cutter, and a food server,” Endozo said.
Born and raised in a remote area, Endozo grew up in a small nipa hut with no electricity, with the nearest water source at least half a kilometer away. He has eight siblings, and his father worked as a carpenter in their barangay.
“Even as a young child, I already understood how hard our life was. We considered ourselves lucky if we could eat three times a day, or if we had any viand to go with our rice. I attended elementary school in our barangay, which meant walking more than a kilometer every morning, then walking back home at noon for lunch, because we couldn’t bring packed meals. Our parents often didn’t even know whether there would be anything for us to eat at midday. Many times, our meal was nothing more than rice and salt,” narrated Endozo .
He finished elementary school having had money to buy something during recess “only a handful of times.”
“I never experienced owning a new school bag; most of the time, I used an old hand-me-down one or even a fishing net,” he added.
Despite these hardships, the Endozo siblings became known at their barangay public school for their strong academic performance.
“That academic excellence became my bridge to continuing my education at a high school in the town proper,” he said.
Endozo earned a scholarship to a private high school in the town proper, though getting there was far from easy. Because his parents couldn’t afford the fare, he had to walk at least three kilometers every day just to reach the main road where he could catch a ride.
He owned only two school uniforms throughout high school. “I never had a textbook of my own and relied entirely on books borrowed from the library,” he shared.
“My daily allowance was always just enough to cover my fare to and from school and a small viand to go with the rice I brought from home. For four years, I lived on mongo soup and pancit habhab as viand.”
After graduating from high school with flying colors, he faced a daunting question: What’s next?
He knew education was his only way out of poverty, yet his family could not afford college. So, he set off for Oman.
“Eventually, I landed my first job in a hotel. From that moment, I never stopped learning. I began setting my sights on the next available position, working hard to be recognized and considered for promotion,” Endozo said.
“Step by step, I rose through the ranks: from waiter to captain, then supervisor, restaurant manager, operations manager, department head, director, and finally general manager.”
He proved to those around him that he deserved every promotion. Competing against professionals of many different nationalities without a college degree or formal background in hospitality, Endozo faced challenges at every turn — yet he prevailed.
Throughout his career, Endozo has worked with some of the world’s most prestigious hotel brands, including InterContinental Hotels, Burj Al Arab, Jumeirah Group, Raffles Hotels, Millennium Hotels, Hilton Worldwide, Citadines, The Ascott, and Fraser Hospitality.
Once he began earning steady money, Endozo started helping his siblings move to Dubai. Eventually, six of them landed good jobs in the city.
“After that, I helped my nephews and nieces, then cousins, then distant relatives, and later even people from our barangay. What started with one person became a chain reaction of helping one another, and today there are more than 120 of us from our family and community working in Dubai,” he said.
Everyone has a story, and Endozo’s shows that poverty and a lack of early resources are not dead ends to reaching your dreams.
Michael Banua holds a degree in chemistry, though he eventually realized his real passion lay elsewhere: storytelling— where his true chemistry is.
Today, Banua is recognized as one of the Top 100 Influencers in the Middle East, with a social media community of more than 230,000 followers as @YourKuyaMico, an award-winning, mentor-driven content platform in the UAE.
It all started during the COVID-19 pandemic with just AED 500 to his name after the company where he worked announced it was shutting down.
“Since I couldn’t travel, I started posting old food photos from my gallery. To my surprise, these received great engagement and positive reactions. Soon, brands noticed my work and began sending complimentary meals in exchange for content,” Banua said.
His very first restaurant review featured a small cafeteria in Karama that served him an AED 12 biryani.
“One day, a restaurant near our office asked how much I charged. Without knowing the industry rates, I confidently said AED 150. That became my first paid collaboration and made me realize content creation could actually become a career,” Banua said.
One of his first major collaborations was with a Dubai bottled drinking water company. The campaign brief arrived at 10 pm, and the content had to be delivered by lunchtime the next day.
“Instead of creating a traditional advertisement, I documented my real routine as an OFW — from waking up, preparing for work, commuting on the Metro, spending the day in the office, and ending the day creating food content — while naturally integrating [the bottled water brand] into the story. The campaign stood out because it felt authentic and story-driven rather than promotional,” said Banua.
He landed a follow-up contract with the company, with the campaign appearing on billboards across the UAE — including along Sheikh Zayed Road, the main highway artery — as well as on buses, the Dubai Metro, YouTube ads, cinemas, and other nationwide marketing materials.
That campaign proved to be the turning point in Banua’s career, opening doors to new opportunities — including an invitation from the Dubai Media Office (DMO) to join the #BrandDubai and #DubaiDestinations campaigns promoting the city to the world.
Today, Banua works with leading government entities and brands, including Brand Dubai, Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, Dubai Culture, Sharjah Tourism, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs (GDRFA), the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA), Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC), Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), Miral (Yas Island), Majid Al Futtaim, and Big Ticket.
More importantly, Banua has been paying his success forward by educating and mentoring aspiring content creators inspired by his journey.
“I continue to conduct workshops, with my latest initiative focused on helping Filipino content creators better understand the UAE influencer and content creation landscape,” said Banua, who wears barong tagalog to major events, television appearances, speaking engagements, and UAE campaigns — even those unrelated to the Filipino community — “because representing my culture is something I deeply value.”
“At the heart of everything I do is storytelling, mentorship, and proudly representing the Filipino community while inspiring others to pursue their passions and create opportunities for themselves,” he added. – Rappler.com
